articles.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
articles.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.
articles.content:
Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.

Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing."

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion

For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!"

Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space."

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome

This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

These surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao."

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.

The merger has left astronomers with another important question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

The telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

Scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.

Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

articles.personality_title: James Webb telescope captures a rare star merger in Andromeda galaxy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the Andromeda galaxy, two stars were orbiting each other for thousands of years. One was a giant star much bigger and brighter than our Sun, and the other was smaller, about 70% the mass of the Sun. Scientists have long wanted to understand what happens when such stars collide and merge.

**What happened** – In 2025, astronomers observed the smaller star spiraling into the giant star, causing a sudden, bright eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope took detailed pictures just 47 days after this event. Combining Webb’s data with earlier observations, scientists saw how the two stars merged into one, creating a new star nicknamed Bao.

**Impact** – This is the first time astronomers have watched a star merger so closely and soon after it happened. The event showed that the merger process can be much faster and more explosive than expected. It also revealed how stars can change by sharing and losing material. Understanding these mergers helps explain how some stars become extreme objects like neutron stars or black holes.

**What's next step** – Researchers will keep observing Bao to learn how it changes over time and to better understand how merged stars evolve. New telescopes, like NASA’s upcoming Roman Space Telescope, will help find more merging stars, giving scientists more chances to study these rare cosmic events.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using the James Webb Space Telescope, scientists have directly observed a rare and fast star merger in the Andromeda galaxy, opening a new window into how stars live and change.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le télescope James Webb capture une rare fusion d’étoiles dans la galaxie d’Andromède
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans la galaxie d’Andromède, deux étoiles tournaient l’une autour de l’autre depuis des milliers d’années. L’une était une étoile géante, bien plus grande et brillante que notre Soleil, l’autre plus petite, environ 70 % de la masse du Soleil. Les scientifiques voulaient comprendre ce qui se passe quand ces étoiles entrent en collision et fusionnent.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2025, les astronomes ont observé l’étoile plus petite s’enfoncer dans la géante, provoquant une éruption lumineuse soudaine. Le télescope spatial James Webb de la NASA a pris des images détaillées seulement 47 jours après cet événement. En combinant les données de Webb avec des observations antérieures, les scientifiques ont vu comment les deux étoiles ont fusionné en une seule, surnommée Bao.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que les astronomes observent aussi de près et si rapidement une fusion d’étoiles. Cet événement a montré que la fusion peut être beaucoup plus rapide et explosive que prévu. Il a aussi révélé comment les étoiles changent en partageant et en perdant de la matière. Comprendre ces fusions aide à expliquer comment certaines étoiles deviennent des objets extrêmes comme les étoiles à neutrons ou les trous noirs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à observer Bao pour comprendre son évolution et mieux saisir comment les étoiles fusionnées changent avec le temps. De nouveaux télescopes, comme le futur télescope spatial Roman de la NASA, aideront à découvrir plus d’étoiles en fusion, donnant plus d’occasions d’étudier ces événements rares.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Grâce au télescope James Webb, les scientifiques ont observé directement une fusion d’étoiles rare et rapide dans la galaxie d’Andromède, ouvrant une nouvelle voie pour comprendre la vie et l’évolution des étoiles.
articles.personality_title_es: El telescopio James Webb captura una rara fusión de estrellas en la galaxia de Andrómeda
articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03803-8European and Japanese probes will trace different paths around the planet to study its surface and its surroundings.
articles.content:
False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–2015 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

On 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, says Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

One mission, two orbiters

For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

The BepiColumbo spacecraft (illustration).Credit: ESA - P. Carril

Travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo launched in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the successful arrival of the BepiColombo spacecraft at Mercury after an eight-year journey, marking only the second mission to orbit the planet. This achievement represents a significant milestone in space exploration with broad scientific implications for understanding Mercury and the inner solar system. The article provides detailed context about the mission's instruments, objectives, and future plans, demonstrating substantial substance and real-world impact.
articles.personality_title: BepiColombo spacecraft arrives at Mercury after eight years of travel
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, and reaching it is very difficult because spacecraft must slow down enough to enter its orbit. Before BepiColombo, only one mission, NASA’s MESSENGER, had orbited Mercury.

**What happened** – On November 21, 2026, the BepiColombo spacecraft, a joint project by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), successfully entered orbit around Mercury after traveling for eight years. The spacecraft has two scientific probes: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO). They will separate soon to study different parts of Mercury from different heights.

**Impact** – This mission is special because it uses new instruments like the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), the first X-ray camera sent on an interplanetary mission. BepiColombo will gather detailed information about Mercury’s surface, magnetic field, and how the solar wind affects it. This will help scientists understand the planet’s history and environment better than ever before.

**What's next step** – The two probes will split in early December. MIO will orbit higher to study Mercury’s magnetic field, while MPO will move closer to the surface by March 2027 to analyze the planet’s surface. The data collected will be used for years to deepen our knowledge of Mercury.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After a long journey, BepiColombo has reached Mercury to study the planet with advanced instruments, promising new discoveries about our solar system’s closest planet.
articles.personality_title_fr: La sonde BepiColombo atteint Mercure après huit ans de voyage
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Mercure est la planète la plus proche du Soleil, et y parvenir est très difficile car les sondes doivent ralentir suffisamment pour entrer en orbite. Avant BepiColombo, seule une mission, MESSENGER de la NASA, avait orbité autour de Mercure.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le 21 novembre 2026, la sonde BepiColombo, un projet commun de l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) et de l’Agence japonaise d’exploration aérospatiale (JAXA), est entrée avec succès en orbite autour de Mercure après huit ans de voyage. La sonde comprend deux modules scientifiques : l’orbiteur planétaire Mercury (MPO) de l’ESA et l’orbiteur magnétosphérique Mercury (MIO) de la JAXA. Ils vont bientôt se séparer pour étudier différentes zones de Mercure à différentes altitudes.

**Impact** – Cette mission est spéciale car elle utilise de nouveaux instruments comme le spectromètre d’imagerie X de Mercure (MIXS), la première caméra à rayons X envoyée lors d’une mission interplanétaire. BepiColombo recueillera des informations détaillées sur la surface de Mercure, son champ magnétique et l’impact du vent solaire. Cela aidera les scientifiques à mieux comprendre l’histoire et l’environnement de la planète.

**Prochaine étape** – Les deux sondes se sépareront début décembre. MIO orbitera plus haut pour étudier le champ magnétique de Mercure, tandis que MPO descendra plus près de la surface d’ici mars 2027 pour analyser la planète. Les données collectées seront utilisées pendant des années pour approfondir nos connaissances sur Mercure.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après un long voyage, BepiColombo a atteint Mercure pour étudier la planète avec des instruments avancés, promettant de nouvelles découvertes sur la planète la plus proche du Soleil.
articles.personality_title_es: La nave BepiColombo llega a Mercurio tras ocho años de viaje
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Mercurio es el planeta más cercano al Sol y llegar hasta él es muy difícil porque las naves deben reducir su velocidad para entrar en órbita. Antes de BepiColombo, solo una misión, MESSENGER de la NASA, había orbitado Mercurio.

**Qué pasó** – El 21 de noviembre de 2026, la nave BepiColombo, un proyecto conjunto de la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) y la Agencia de Exploración Aeroespacial de Japón (JAXA), logró entrar en órbita alrededor de Mercurio después de un viaje de ocho años. La nave tiene dos sondas científicas: la Orbiter Planetario de Mercurio (MPO) de la ESA y la Orbiter Magnetosférico de Mercurio (MIO) de JAXA. Pronto se separarán para estudiar diferentes partes de Mercurio desde distintas alturas.

**Impacto** – Esta misión es especial porque usa instrumentos nuevos como el Espectrómetro de Imagen de Rayos X de Mercurio (MIXS), la primera cámara de rayos X enviada en una misión interplanetaria. BepiColombo recogerá información detallada sobre la superficie de Mercurio, su campo magnético y cómo lo afecta el viento solar. Esto ayudará a los científicos a entender mejor la historia y el entorno del planeta.

**Próximo paso** – Las dos sondas se separarán a principios de diciembre. MIO orbitará más alto para estudiar el campo magnético de Mercurio, mientras que MPO descenderá cerca de la superficie para analizarla a partir de marzo de 2027. Los datos recogidos se usarán durante años para ampliar nuestro conocimiento sobre Mercurio.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Después de un largo viaje, BepiColombo ha llegado a Mercurio para estudiarlo con instrumentos avanzados, prometiendo nuevos descubrimientos sobre el planeta más cercano al Sol.

articles.title: Claude, find me a planet: amateur astronomers are using AI with mixed results
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03790-wArtificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to identify previously unknown exoplanet candidates — some more credible than others.
articles.content:
Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to find undiscovered exoplanets (artist’s illustration).Credit: Hypersphere/SPL

In September, Pavel Rabtsevich sat down at his computer and asked an AI model to discover a planet. Rabtsevich directed the program to a specific batch of telescope data and gave it a high-level plan to hunt for evidence of undetected planets. In about two weeks, the program delivered the goods: two possible planets orbiting a star 116 light years from Earth. Professional astronomers are now checking the findings.

History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI

Rabtsevich, who works in Spain as an artificial-intelligence specialist and has no formal astronomy education, is one of the most successful of a wave of amateur astronomers who are using AI models to search for worlds outside the Solar System. Citizen scientists have been using publicly available tools from NASA and other researchers to find planets for decades. But AI’s ability to scour the Internet for such tools and use them to process massive amounts of data has lowered the barrier to entry for non-specialists who want to become planet hunters.

The newfound accessibility of data-analysis tools, however, has meant that not all amateurs are doing research responsibly, says Michelle Kunimoto, an exoplanet researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada. Some planet hunters don’t fully understand the algorithms being used by AI tools and thus can’t validate the models’ findings, Kunimoto says. “There’s been a huge, overwhelming surge of AI-driven papers, which tend to have [planet] candidates that are not the best quality,” they say. And as a result, “the systems we use to disseminate science are being overwhelmed”.

An AI astronomer

For his search, Rabtsevich enlisted Claude Code, an AI coding tool made by Anthropic. He asked it to sift through data from more than 120,000 stars observed by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) in late 2025 and early 2026. He guided Claude to use a popular planet-detection algorithm to search for dips in the stars’ brightness. A regular and repeated dimming of a star can be a sign that a planet is orbiting it and blocking a little bit of light every time it passes between the star and an observer.

Claude zeroed in on a star called TIC 4206066, which showed two separate cycles of dimming, one roughly every 3 days and another every 11 days. That suggests that TIC 4206066 is orbited by two planets, one of which loops around the star more tightly than the other and thus takes less time to complete a full rotation.

These alien planets are astronomers’ favourites

Rabtsevich instructed Claude to look for those same repetitive patterns in archival TESS data. Sure enough, data from 2018 and 2020 recorded the same pattern of dimming coming from TIC 4206066. At Rabtsevich’s direction, Claude then found a planet-detection algorithm, one written and made publicly available by Kunimoto, and ran it to validate the signals.

Rabtsevich published his findings to the platform Zenodo as a preprint1 on 25 September. His work has not been peer reviewed, but TESS astronomers have completed an independent analysis of the signals and have added them to their official list of planet candidates.
articles.reasoning: The article describes how AI tools are enabling amateur astronomers to discover new exoplanet candidates, lowering barriers to scientific discovery and expanding participation in space exploration. The findings have been independently validated and added to official records, indicating real scientific progress with broad inspirational impact.
articles.personality_title: Amateur astronomers use AI to find new planets beyond our solar system
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, professional scientists have searched for planets outside our solar system, called exoplanets, using data from space telescopes. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) tools have become available to the public, allowing amateur astronomers to join the search.

**What happened** – In September 2026, Pavel Rabtsevich, an AI expert without formal astronomy training, used an AI program named Claude Code to analyze data from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Over two weeks, the AI helped him find signs of two new possible planets orbiting a star 116 light years away. These planets were detected by spotting regular dips in the star’s brightness, which happens when a planet passes in front of it. Professional scientists have since checked and confirmed these findings, officially adding them to the list of planet candidates.

**Impact** – This discovery shows how AI can help people without special astronomy training contribute to important space research. By making complex data easier to analyze, AI lowers the barrier for more people to participate in scientific discoveries. However, experts warn that not all amateurs fully understand the AI tools, which can lead to less reliable results. Still, the success of Rabtsevich and Claude Code highlights the potential for AI to expand who can explore space.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will continue to review and study the new planet candidates to learn more about their characteristics. Meanwhile, more citizen scientists are likely to use AI tools to explore telescope data, potentially finding more exoplanets. Researchers also hope to improve AI methods and provide better guidance so that discoveries are accurate and trustworthy.
